Sample Size Planning From the AIPE Perspective for the Mean of a Crossed Design of Units and Raters

Source: R/ss_aipe_crossed.R
ss_aipe_crossed.Rd

Plans the numbers of units and raters for a fully crossed design, in which every rater scores every unit once, so that the confidence interval for the mean score is sufficiently narrow at the least cost. The units are the objects of measurement (persons, essays, recordings, or the topics of an information retrieval evaluation) and the raters are whoever or whatever produces the scores (judges, coders, assessors, or automated scoring models). When the raters are a sample from a population of raters, as the units are a sample of units, the interval for the population mean carries the variability of both samples, and no number of units can make up for too few raters. The interval planned for is the one ci_crossed computes from the data.

Usage

ss_aipe_crossed(
  true_var_unit,
  true_var_rater,
  true_var_residual,
  width,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  assurance = NULL,
  n_raters = NULL,
  unit_cost = 0,
  rater_cost = 0,
  judgment_cost = 1,
  quantile = c("t", "normal"),
  max_units = 1e+05,
  max_raters = 500
)

Arguments

true_var_unit, true_var_rater, true_var_residual

Planning values of the three variance components: of the unit effects (\(\sigma^2_u\), how much units differ in their mean score over the population of raters), of the rater effects (\(\sigma^2_r\), how much raters differ in leniency), and of the residuals (\(\sigma^2_e\), the unit by rater interaction together with error, which one score per cell cannot separate). The first two must be nonnegative and the third positive. The var_unit, var_rater, and var_residual rows of ci_crossed applied to a pilot array estimate them.

width

Desired full width of the confidence interval for the mean.

conf_level

Confidence level of the interval (default 0.95).

assurance

Optional probability, strictly between 0 and 1, that the realized interval is no wider than width. The default NULL plans for the width at the planning values. A plan with an assurance is never smaller than the plan without one (see Details), so an assurance at or below one half returns the plan without one. An assurance requires quantile = "t", since it concerns the sampling variability of the estimated variance that the t quantile accounts for.

n_raters

Optional fixed number of raters (a whole number of at least 2), for a study whose panel of raters is already set; only the number of units is then planned. The default NULL plans both.

unit_cost, rater_cost, judgment_cost

Costs of adding a unit, of recruiting a rater, and of one judgment (one rater's score of one unit), in any common currency. A design with \(n_u\) units and \(n_r\) raters costs \(c_u n_u + c_r n_r + c_j n_u n_r\). The defaults 0, 0, and 1 make the cost the number of judgments, so the plan is the design that collects the fewest scores. The costs must be nonnegative and not all zero.

quantile

"t" (the default) or "normal": the quantile the planned interval is formed with (see Details).

max_units, max_raters

The largest numbers of units and of raters the search considers. Defaults 100000 and 500.

Value

A data.frame (class dmar_ss_aipe) with rows necessary_n_units and necessary_n_raters (the design; the second is specified_n_raters when n_raters was supplied), total_judgments (\(n_u n_r\), the number of scores to collect), cost, expected_width (the full width of the interval at the planning values, at most width; a plan with an assurance guards against an unlucky sample, so its expected width is no wider, and narrower once the assurance asks for more than the plan without one delivers), df (the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom the interval will have at the planned design, computed from the planning values), rater_floor (see Details), the echoes true_var_unit, true_var_rater, true_var_residual, width, and conf_level, and assurance when one was supplied. The quantile the plan used is the "quantile" attribute. tidy() reports the number of units as the sample size, and glance() keeps every row.

Details

The model and the variance of the mean. The score of unit \(u\) by rater \(r\) is \(y_{ur} = \mu + a_u + b_r + e_{ur}\), with independent unit effects, rater effects, and residuals of mean zero and variances \(\sigma^2_u\), \(\sigma^2_r\), and \(\sigma^2_e\). Both units and raters are random, so the target is \(\mu\), the mean over the population of units and the population of raters, and the grand mean of a complete array of \(n_u\) units by \(n_r\) raters has variance $$V = \frac{\sigma^2_u}{n_u} + \frac{\sigma^2_r}{n_r} + \frac{\sigma^2_e}{n_u n_r}.$$ In the vocabulary of generalizability theory (Brennan, 2001) the units are the objects of measurement and the raters a random facet crossed with them.

The rater floor. Whatever the number of units, \(V\) is at least \(\sigma^2_r / n_r\), so with \(n_r\) raters the half-width cannot fall below \(z\,\sigma_r / \sqrt{n_r}\), with \(z\) the normal quantile. A design meeting a target half-width \(h\) (half of width) under the normal quantile therefore needs more than \(z^2 \sigma^2_r / h^2\) raters; that number is the rater_floor row. The t quantile raises the requirement further. When raters vary, adding units cannot make up for a panel that is too small, and a plan with n_raters at or below the floor is refused with that explanation.

The interval planned for. ci_crossed estimates \(V\) by the ANOVA estimates of the three components, a negative estimate truncated at zero, and refers the grand mean to a t distribution whose degrees of freedom are Satterthwaite's (1946) for that combination of mean squares. With quantile = "t", the default, the plan forms the interval the same way at the planning values: the planned half-width is \(t_{\nu} \sqrt{V}\), where the degrees of freedom \(\nu\) are those of the plug-in estimate \((MS_u + MS_r - MS_e) / (n_u n_r)\) computed from the expected mean squares. With quantile = "normal" the planned half-width is \(z \sqrt{V}\), the half-width of an interval whose variance is known; quantile = "normal" reproduces planning that uses the normal quantile. Its designs are smaller, and because the analysis interval uses the t quantile, its realized intervals exceed the target width more often than those of a plan made with the t quantile. The gap is largest when the rater component is at or near zero. The normal plan then uses two raters, since raters add nothing to \(V\), but the analysis still estimates the rater component from those two. With no rater variance, \(MS_r\) exceeds \(MS_e\) by chance in about a third of samples and the estimate is kept; the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom then fall, to one or two when the unit component is small beside the residual one, and the interval can be several times wider than the target. The t plan sees the few degrees of freedom two raters give at the planning values and adds raters or units to make up for them. ss_aipe_crossed_sensitivity shows how a given plan fares.

Assurance. The plan without an assurance gives an interval no wider than the target at the planning values, and the realized interval is narrower or wider as the estimated variance falls below or above \(V\). An assurance \(\gamma\) (Kelley & Maxwell, 2003) asks instead for a realized width at most width with probability at least \(\gamma\). The plan approximates the distribution of the plug-in variance by a scaled chi square on the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, as Satterthwaite (1946) does, and requires $$t_{\nu} \sqrt{V \max(1, q_{\gamma} / \nu)} \le h,$$ with \(q_{\gamma}\) the \(\gamma\) quantile of the chi square distribution on \(\nu\) degrees of freedom. Under the same approximation the plan without an assurance already meets the target with probability at least \(P(\chi^2_{\nu} \le \nu)\), which exceeds one half because the median of a chi square lies below its mean: about .58 at \(\nu = 5\), .53 at \(\nu = 30\), and nearer one half as \(\nu\) grows. An assurance at or below that probability asks for nothing more, and \(q_{\gamma} / \nu\) is then at most 1; taking the larger of 1 and \(q_{\gamma} / \nu\) keeps such an assurance from shrinking the design. The rule is that a plan with an assurance is never smaller than the plan without one: it costs at least as much, and with a fixed panel it has at least as many units. An assurance at or below one half always returns the plan without one.

The search. For every number of raters from 2 to max_raters (or for n_raters alone) the planner finds the smallest number of units that meets the target, prices each such design, and returns the cheapest; designs of equal cost are resolved toward fewer raters. With the t quantile the planned width is not monotone in the number of units: as units are added, \(V\) approaches its rater floor while the degrees of freedom eventually fall toward \(n_r - 1\), and past some point the larger quantile outweighs the smaller variance, so more units lengthen the planned interval. The search therefore looks for the smallest feasible number of units on the stretch where the planned width is still falling, and it counts a number of raters as infeasible when the shortest interval that number allows is too wide. A warning says so when the cheapest design found uses max_raters raters, since a larger limit might find a cheaper one. When no design within the limits meets the target, the error names the limit that binds: if more units would do, it gives the design they would allow and points to max_units; otherwise more raters are needed, and it says whether the reason is the rater floor or the loss of degrees of freedom under the t quantile.

A closed form for the allocation. The search needs no closed form, but one special case has one, which serves as a check. When only judgments cost (unit_cost = 0, rater_cost = 0), the problem of minimizing \(V\) for a fixed number of judgments has the form Marcoulides and Goldstein (1990) solved for a two-facet generalizability study, whose error variance is \(\sigma^2_1 / n_1 + \sigma^2_2 / n_2 + \sigma^2_{12} / (n_1 n_2)\) under a budget on \(n_1 n_2\): the optimum has \(n_1 / n_2 = \sigma^2_1 / \sigma^2_2\) (their Equations 5 and 6). Here that is \(n_u / n_r = \sigma^2_u / \sigma^2_r\). The cost is flat near the optimum, so the least costly design in whole numbers can stray from that ratio while collecting barely more judgments than the continuous optimum.

An information retrieval evaluation. In a comparison of two retrieval systems over a set of topics, each judged by a set of relevance assessors (people, or automated judges such as language models), the units are the topics, the raters are the assessors, and each cell holds the difference between the two systems' effectiveness scores on the topic as computed from that assessor's judgments. The grand mean is then the mean difference between the systems over the populations of topics and assessors, and true_var_unit and true_var_rater describe how much the difference between the systems varies over topics and over assessors (the topic by system and assessor by system interactions).

When the planning values are uncertain. The plan is only as good as the planning values, and a rater component that is underestimated is costly, since it governs the floor. ss_aipe_crossed_sensitivity shows by Monte Carlo simulation what a plan delivers when the true components differ from the planning values. When no trustworthy planning values exist, a two-stage sequential procedure, in which a pilot array determines the final numbers of units and raters, can take their place.

References

Brennan, R. L. (2001). Generalizability theory. Springer. doi:10.1007/978-1-4757-3456-0

Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2003). Sample size for multiple regression: Obtaining regression coefficients that are accurate, not simply significant. Psychological Methods, 8(3), 305–321. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.8.3.305

Marcoulides, G. A., & Goldstein, Z. (1990). The optimization of generalizability studies with resource constraints. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 50(4), 761–768. doi:10.1177/0013164490504004

Satterthwaite, F. E. (1946). An approximate distribution of estimates of variance components. Biometrics Bulletin, 2(6), 110–114. doi:10.2307/3002019

See also

ci_crossed for the interval the plan is for, ss_aipe_crossed_sensitivity for what a plan delivers when the planning values are wrong, and icc for the reliability of a single rater's scores in the same design.

Examples

# Essays scored by raters. Planning values: essays differ with
# variance 0.50, raters differ in leniency with variance 0.10, and the
# residual variance is 0.40. The goal is a 95% interval no wider than
# 0.40 for the mean score; by default the plan collects the fewest
# scores.
ss_aipe_crossed(true_var_unit = 0.50, true_var_rater = 0.10, true_var_residual = 0.40,
                width = 0.40)
#>  term               value 
#>  necessary_n_units  94    
#>  necessary_n_raters 22    
#>  total_judgments    2068  
#>  cost               2068  
#>  expected_width     0.400 
#>  df                 72.459
#>  rater_floor        9.604 
#>  true_var_unit      0.500 
#>  true_var_rater     0.100 
#>  true_var_residual  0.400 
#>  width              0.400 
#>  conf_level         0.950 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# Recruiting and training a rater costs as much as 40 scores, so the
# cheapest design uses fewer raters and more essays.
ss_aipe_crossed(true_var_unit = 0.50, true_var_rater = 0.10, true_var_residual = 0.40,
                width = 0.40, rater_cost = 40, judgment_cost = 1)
#>  term               value 
#>  necessary_n_units  112   
#>  necessary_n_raters 19    
#>  total_judgments    2128  
#>  cost               2888  
#>  expected_width     0.399 
#>  df                 53.264
#>  rater_floor        9.604 
#>  true_var_unit      0.500 
#>  true_var_rater     0.100 
#>  true_var_residual  0.400 
#>  width              0.400 
#>  conf_level         0.950 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# A panel of 30 raters is already set: plan the essays only, with 80%
# assurance that the interval is no wider than 0.40.
ss_aipe_crossed(true_var_unit = 0.50, true_var_rater = 0.10, true_var_residual = 0.40,
                width = 0.40, n_raters = 30, assurance = 0.80)
#>  term               value  
#>  necessary_n_units  89     
#>  specified_n_raters 30     
#>  total_judgments    2670   
#>  cost               2670   
#>  expected_width     0.378  
#>  df                 104.006
#>  rater_floor        9.604  
#>  true_var_unit      0.500  
#>  true_var_rater     0.100  
#>  true_var_residual  0.400  
#>  width              0.400  
#>  conf_level         0.950  
#>  assurance          0.800  
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
